indigenous.label: Indigenous-authored history & critique
indigenous.date_label: Earlier witnesses 1615–1938 · critiques of the academy 1969–99 · refusal, resurgence and peoplehood 2007–17
indigenous.description: Historical writing, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors, from early manuscript and print witnesses to academic history and political theory. It is plural: Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Dakota, Māori, Hawaiian and Aboriginal traditions have their own roots and are not branches of one academic field. From 1969 Deloria, Adams, LaRocque, Sioui, Trask and Smith turned criticism on the institutions and disciplines that studied them; LaRocque judged that 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (1999). After 2000 the criticism became theory: Audra Simpson's 'ethnographic refusal' (2007, 2014); Coulthard's case against 'the politics of recognition' (2009, 2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson's resurgence, which turns from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy' toward 'a resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems' (2014); Andersen's Métis 'peoplehood' against 'mixedness' (2014). Older university scholarship about Indigenous peoples and community-engaged research have their own entries; settler colonial studies is a comparative field.
indigenous.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier witnesses: Guaman Poma (c. 1615/1616), Cusick (checked 1828 edition), Apess (1836), Te Rangikāheke (manuscripts before 1854), Warren (1885), Thunderchild and Ahenakew (1923; 1929), Pei Te Hurinui Jones (1929), Mathews (1932, 1961), Te Rangi Hīroa (1938, 1949), McNickle (1949; Native American Tribalism, 1973). Critiques 1969–99: Deloria, Custer Died for Your Sins (1969); Adams, Prison of Grass (1975); LaRocque, Defeathering the Indian (1975) and her dissertation (1999); Dickason (1984, 1992); Sioui (1989); Walker (1990); Trask, 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and From a Native Daughter (1993); Kameʻeleihiwa (1992); Wilson (1996); O'Brien (1997); Rigney (1999); Smith, Decolonizing Methodologies (1999). After 2000: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) and Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Coulthard, Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017); Andersen, 'Métis' (2014); Moreton-Robinson, The White Possessive (2015). See the strands for works, collaborators and evidence limits.

representative_people.context: Self-determination shapes who asks questions and controls research; her situated account acknowledges critical/feminist resources and differing insider/outsider positions.
representative_people.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999); with Judith Simon (eds.), A Civilising Mission? (2001)

representative_people.context: Māori historical interpretation and political struggle in Aotearoa New Zealand; one regionally situated contribution.
representative_people.works: Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou: Struggle Without End (1990)

representative_people.context: Natick land loss and strategic kinship/institutional adaptation challenge an uncomplicated disappearance narrative.
representative_people.works: Dispossession by Degrees: Indian Land and Identity in Natick, Massachusetts, 1650–1790 (1997)

representative_people.context: Māori scholarship joins historical interpretation and material-culture research; an earlier trajectory distinct from later methodological manifestos.
representative_people.works: Vikings of the Sunrise (1938); The Coming of the Maori (1949)

representative_people.context: A Native American manifesto challenges social scientists and institutions; its particular arguments await primary chapter review. As a 1965 guest speaker he criticised the McNickle-organised workshops (Beck 1995, mediated).
representative_people.works: Custer Died for Your Sins (1969)

representative_people.context: Wahpetonwan Dakota historian argues for tribal and family historians’ authority, sustained relationships and careful interpretation of transmitted knowledge.
representative_people.works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

representative_people.context: Australian Indigenist research methodology is a distinct bibliographic inclusion; detailed principles await the primary article.
representative_people.works: “Internationalization of an Indigenous Anticolonial Cultural Critique…” (1999)

representative_people.context: Andean manuscript chronicler addressed a Christian colonial order and royal government. A selected early historical practice, not the founder of a single modern Indigenous method or evidence of a direct line to THOA.
representative_people.works: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (manuscript c. 1615/1616)

representative_people.context: Tuscarora writer assembled Six Nations histories and translated materials into English; his 1828 preface makes the act of historical writing visible. The checked second edition does not establish an absolute beginning for Haudenosaunee knowledge.
representative_people.works: Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (checked second edition, 1828)

representative_people.context: His historical address reinterprets King Philip’s War, criticizes colonial violence and questions Pilgrim commemoration through a Christian moral argument. This is an earlier intervention in historical narration, not a claim that later writers borrowed directly from him.
representative_people.works: Eulogy on King Philip (1836), selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Collected histories from relatives and tribal leaders and addressed a nineteenth-century white readership. The publisher’s account retains his goals and limitations; recording oral knowledge is not equivalent to the later decolonizing programme.
representative_people.works: History of the Ojibway People (first publication, 1885)

representative_people.context: Māori manuscripts written before 1854 connect genealogy, historical narration and land. Te Ara documents Grey’s unacknowledged reuse and alterations; the Indigenous author is retained alongside the history of colonial publication.
representative_people.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

representative_people.context: Recorded Chief Thunderchild’s narratives in Cree in 1923 and wrote through Old Keyam’s literary voice. The 1973 book passed through Ruth M. Buck’s editing; composition, narration and publication are distinct. His 1929 folklore article supplies an interwar publication milestone.
representative_people.works: Thunderchild recordings (1923); Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973, edited by Ruth M. Buck)

representative_people.context: Named Plains Cree narrator whose histories Ahenakew recorded in 1923. His knowledge-producing role is separate from Ahenakew’s writing and the later editor’s selection; he is not an anonymous informant or the fictional Old Keyam.
representative_people.works: Narratives recorded in 1923, published in Part I of Voices of the Plains Cree (1973)

representative_people.context: The 1995 introduction discusses Cree interpretation and challenges the editor’s exclusion of a story he translated. This supplies a specific criticism of editorial mediation, distinct from Thunderchild’s narration and Ahenakew’s authorship.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the 1995 edition of Voices of the Plains Cree, especially p. xii

representative_people.context: Recorded Tainui genealogies and historical traditions in Māori and English. Te Ara distinguishes his 1929 publication, English manuscript by about 1936, contested reuse by Kelly and the 1995 posthumous history.
representative_people.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

representative_people.context: Her historical scholarship examines European representations and places First Peoples within a broad Canadian historical synthesis. MNO recognizes her Métis contribution. She is one major historian within a wider field, not its sole origin.
representative_people.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992)

representative_people.context: Métis scholar’s critique of Canadian colonialism joins historical interpretation and Marxist politics. The institutional biography dates his doctorate and university appointment to 1966; detailed book arguments remain outside this description-level inclusion.
representative_people.works: Prison of Grass: Canada from a Native Point of View (1975)

representative_people.context: Her 1999 dissertation relates her 1974 research on stereotypes in Alberta history and social-studies texts to Defeathering the Indian and names its targets in Canadian historiography: Walker's survey ('not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui ('a language of containment') and the cross-cultural approach of Brown and Van Kirk. Distinct from Adams, on whom she draws.
representative_people.works: Defeathering the Indian (1975); Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices… (1999), selected passage; When the Other Is Me (2011)

representative_people.context: In his 1991 interview, explains autohistory as bringing Indigenous self-interpretation and transmitted traditions into historical discourse. His moral and philosophical proposal is situated; its account of Amerindian values does not define every nation.
representative_people.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

representative_people.context: Enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993. Historical synthesis and institution-building: They Came Here First (1949) and Native American Tribalism (1973), whose preface challenged 'the certainty that native America had vanished'; a founder of the NCAI (1944), organiser of the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and a creator of the Newberry centre (1972), which he directed in its first fellowship year (1973–74). Not a universal field foundation.
representative_people.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972); Native American Tribalism (1973)

representative_people.context: Osage historical writing combines oral accounts, documentary history and community experience in the publisher’s description. The 1932 work and later 1961 history show an earlier trajectory; their genres and historical questions remain distinct.
representative_people.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

representative_people.context: Publisher describes Hawaiian-language historical inquiry into the Māhele and land relations and names earlier Hawaiian intellectual traditions. Hawaiʻi’s historical trajectory is distinct from Māori and continental North American examples. Trask (1991) named her among the Native historians that Keesing had not read.
representative_people.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992)

representative_people.context: Scholar of Hawaiian sovereignty who answered Keesing's 'invention' thesis with genealogy as 'Native forms of history'; Keesing and Linnekin replied in the same issue. From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999) is known through the publisher; later additions are not assigned to the 1993 book.
representative_people.works: From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999); “Natives and Anthropologists” (1991)

representative_people.context: Interview collection brings Aboriginal narrators’ experiences into print. His interviewer/compiler credit does not make him the sole producer of their knowledge; narrator-specific and methodological claims require the interviews.
representative_people.works: Living Black: Blacks Talk to Kevin Gilbert (1977)

representative_people.context: Life writing offers a situated history of family, work, movement and discrimination. The ANU account supports a distinct historical narrative; autobiography is not interchangeable with all transmitted oral traditions.
representative_people.works: Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

representative_people.context: Coauthor of a Saskatchewan historical study of First Nations and the 1885 conflict. Bill Waiser’s outside coauthor credit is explicit. The bibliographic inclusion does not constitute a chapter-level check of its historical interpretations.
representative_people.works: With Bill Waiser, Loyal Till Death: Indians and the North-West Rebellion (1997)

representative_people.context: Reviewed Making Native Space in 2004, judging that it 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and should have 'incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices'; 'Speaking as a First Nations person', she held that Aboriginal peoples 'still have a special place in Canada'.
representative_people.works: Review of Cole Harris, Making Native Space (BC Studies, 2004)

representative_people.context: Challenges a categorical boundary between Indigenous life and modernity through the case of Mary Sully’s art.
representative_people.works: Playing Indian (1998); Indians in Unexpected Places (2004); Becoming Mary Sully: Toward an American Indian Abstract (2019). American Studies: A User’s Guide (2017) is coauthored with Alexander I. Olson and not reassigned as a sole work.

representative_people.context: Reads Guaman Poma’s autoethnographic writing as a selective appropriation of colonial genres and languages for Andean self-representation.
representative_people.works: “Arts of the Contact Zone” (1991); Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992; later second edition separate); Planetary Longings (2022 essay collection).

representative_people.context: Anthropologist who moved 'away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method of research and writing; Mohawk Interruptus (2014) is known through Nicoll's review.
representative_people.works: 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014)

representative_people.context: Political theorist: against 'the politics of recognition'; 'dispossession, not proletarianization'; self-recognition grounded in land (2009 dissertation, read in part; the 2014 book unread at first hand).
representative_people.works: Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009); Red Skin, White Masks (2014)

representative_people.context: Sociologist: Métis peoplehood grounded in Red River against 'mixedness', answering fur-trade historians (2014).
representative_people.works: 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis' (2014)

representative_people.context: Writer and scholar: resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions'; a turn from efforts to 'Indigenize the academy'; 'This colonial refusal should be met with Indigenous refusal' (2014, read), citing Coulthard on recognition and Audra Simpson on refusal.
representative_people.works: Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011); 'Land as pedagogy' (2014); As We Have Always Done (2017)

representative_people.context: Audra Simpson (2007, read) drew on her account of 'differential access to power and historical knowing' and terra nullius; The White Possessive (2015) is known through Nicoll's review, which quotes the introduction: white possession is 'hypervisible' to Indigenous people.
representative_people.works: Talkin' Up to the White Woman (2000); The White Possessive (2015)

representative_people.context: A shared reference of the resurgence writers, not read here: Coulthard names him a mentor (2009); Audra Simpson places his books among the work of 'a cadre of scholars from Kahnawake' (2007, n. 28); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson cites him (2014).
representative_people.works: Heeding the Voices of Our Ancestors (1995); Peace, Power, Righteousness (1999); Wasáse (2005)

indigenous.scope_note: Part 2 of the Indigenous histories family (split in revision 1.201): history, criticism and theory by Indigenous authors. Membership rests on Indigenous authorship or co-authorship sourced person by person, in the author's own words or an institutional or publisher profile (see the people records), never inferred from a name or a topic. Collaborative and community-directed research has its own entry; settler scholarship about Indigenous peoples is in Ethnohistory and Indigenous–newcomer relations; settler colonial studies is a comparative field. Reviewed through 2017. Read in full: Audra Simpson 2007; Trask 1991 with Keesing's reply; Nicoll's 2015 review of Simpson and Moreton-Robinson. Read in part: Coulthard's 2009 dissertation; Leanne Betasamosake Simpson 2014; Andersen 2009 and the introduction of 2014; LaRocque 1999; Iverson's 1993 introduction to McNickle. Known through named readers or publishers only: Mohawk Interruptus, Red Skin, White Masks, The White Possessive, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back, As We Have Always Done, Native Land and Foreign Desires. Works of 2018–24 are not yet surveyed. In Canadian History PhDs Smith is cited by 47, Audra Simpson by 34, Coulthard by 27 and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson by 26, the last three from almost none before 2010 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

strands.title: Māori historical interpretation
strands.focus: Historical struggle and self-determination in Aotearoa New Zealand; the original 1990 project is distinguished from later additions.
strands.works: Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou (1990)

strands.title: Land loss, kinship and the extinction narrative
strands.focus: Natick land loss, kinship and the making of an extinction narrative.
strands.works: Dispossession by Degrees (1997)

strands.title: Authority over research
strands.focus: Self-determination affects questions, methods and knowledge ownership; researcher positions differ within as well as across communities.
strands.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999)

strands.title: Māori scholarship and material culture
strands.focus: An earlier historical/anthropological trajectory, not a precursor stage superseded by one later method.
strands.works: Vikings of the Sunrise (1938); The Coming of the Maori (1949)

strands.title: Criticism of institutions and researchers
strands.focus: Deloria’s manifesto supplies a distinct Native American intervention; specific chapters remain to be read. As a guest speaker in 1965 he criticised the McNickle-organised workshops (Beck 1995, mediated); Audra Simpson cites Custer with Asad and Said for anthropology's place in empire (2007, n. 2).
strands.works: Custer Died for Your Sins (1969)

strands.title: Tribal and family historians
strands.focus: Wilson connects historical interpretation to sustained relationships and authority to share particular knowledge.
strands.works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

strands.title: Australian Indigenist methodology
strands.focus: Rigney’s 1999 article broadens the methodological bibliography; detailed arguments await primary reading.
strands.works: “Internationalization…” (1999)

strands.title: Early Andean manuscript history
strands.focus: An early colonial-period historical manuscript, situated in a Christian and royal political framework. It demonstrates earlier Indigenous-authored historical writing without making a modern field or THOA descend directly from it.
strands.works: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (manuscript c. 1615/1616)

strands.title: Haudenosaunee histories in print
strands.focus: Cusick’s preface presents gathering materials and translation as historical work. The 1828 second edition is a verified witness; printed publication is not the origin of the traditions it recounts.
strands.works: Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (checked second edition, 1828)

strands.title: Historical argument and colonial commemoration
strands.focus: Apess challenges colonial historical judgments and Pilgrim celebration. His Christian moral argument is an earlier intervention; no borrowing by later theorists is asserted.
strands.works: Eulogy on King Philip (1836), selected paragraphs

strands.title: Ojibwe oral knowledge and written history
strands.focus: Warren’s history draws on relatives and tribal leaders while addressing white readers. The publisher’s discussion retains the author’s nineteenth-century assumptions and limitations.
strands.works: History of the Ojibway People (first publication, 1885)

strands.title: Māori manuscript authorship and colonial publication
strands.focus: Te Rangikāheke’s genealogy and historical narration survive within manuscripts and Grey’s altered publications. Attribution reveals an Indigenous author behind texts circulated under a governor’s name.
strands.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

strands.title: Cree narration and interwar writing
strands.focus: Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s 1923 recording and literary writing, his 1929 publication, and the 1973 edited book carry different dates and authorial roles. Cuthand’s 1995 criticism makes editorial selection visible.
strands.works: 1923 narration/recording; Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973; 1995 introduction)

strands.title: Tainui genealogies and historical writing
strands.focus: Jones’s Māori-language historical work and the history of its publication distinguish interwar research from the 1995 posthumous volume. The institutional biography describes disputed reuse of an earlier English manuscript.
strands.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

strands.title: Canadian historical synthesis and regional inquiry
strands.focus: Dickason’s studies of representations and historical synthesis sit alongside Stonechild and Waiser’s Saskatchewan study. These are different scales and collaborations, not one doctrinal programme.
strands.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal Till Death (1997)

strands.title: Métis scholarship and criticism of representation
strands.focus: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions. The dissertation names its targets: James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing ('Canadian historiography is not that benign'), Trigger's foreword to Sioui as 'a language of containment', and the 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk; Adams is her 'Metis historian and social critic' (PDF pp. 47, 119, 135–136, 249). When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.
strands.works: Prison of Grass (1975); Defeathering the Indian (1975)

strands.title: Wendat autohistory and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Sioui’s author interview supplies an explicit historiographical proposal about self-interpretation and oral transmission. His moral account remains attributed and situated; French and English publication dates are distinct.
strands.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

strands.title: Historical synthesis and Native history institutions
strands.focus: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge. His 1973 preface challenged administrators' 'certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress'; Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. He helped found the NCAI (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and directed the Newberry centre in its first fellowship year (1973–74).
strands.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972)

strands.title: Osage historical writing across the century
strands.focus: Mathews’s 1932 work and 1961 history supply earlier and mid-century examples. The publisher describes oral and documentary historical resources; detailed methodological claims await the works.
strands.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

strands.title: Hawaiian land history and sovereignty
strands.focus: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples. In 1991 Trask answered Keesing's charge that Pacific nationalists 'invent' their pasts: genealogy is 'solid evidence from Native forms of history', and Hawaiians do not want 'to be "liberated" from our past'. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'.
strands.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992); From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999)

strands.title: Aboriginal interviews and life writing
strands.focus: Gilbert’s interviews and Ginibi’s autobiography broaden the historical bibliography beyond university monographs. Their forms and authorial positions differ from each other and from community-transmitted oral histories.
strands.works: Living Black (1977); Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

strands.title: Refusal, resurgence and the critique of recognition
strands.focus: Three linked but distinct arguments, each with its own target. Audra Simpson proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' in Iroquois studies and made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus (2014) carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's history and Morgan and Parker's ethnology. Coulthard challenged 'the now commonplace assumption' that colonial relations in Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon against Taylor and reworking Marx: 'dispossession, not proletarianization' shaped Indigenous–state relations (2009; book 2014). Leanne Betasamosake Simpson defined resurgence as 'the rebuilding of Indigenous nations according to our own political, intellectual and cultural traditions' and met the academy's 'colonial refusal' with 'Indigenous refusal' (2014), citing Coulthard on recognition and Simpson on refusal. Alfred's Wasáse (2005) is a shared reference. In the pages read none of them criticises Wolfe.
strands.works: Audra Simpson, 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007), Mohawk Interruptus (2014); Glen Sean Coulthard, Subjects of Empire? (PhD, 2009), Red Skin, White Masks (2014); Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), 'Land as pedagogy' (2014), As We Have Always Done (2017)

strands.title: Peoplehood against mixedness
strands.focus: Andersen argues that Métis are misrecognised 'as a hybrid off-shoot of two races … rather than as an Indigenous people'. To the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us'. Peoplehood rests on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood' (2014). His 2009 essay asks Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using disciplines including history. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall.
strands.works: Chris Andersen, 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014)

date_span.basis: c. 1615/1616 dates the earliest selected manuscript witness, not the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge or a common academic field. Selected nineteenth-century and interwar practices precede the critiques of 1969–99; refusal, resurgence and peoplehood works are selected to 2017 (revision 1.201). Open from revision 1.133: the former 2000 end was the atlas boundary, not an ending.

coverage.basis: Part 2 reviewed on 2026-10-27 through 2017 for Indigenous-authored criticism and theory (Audra Simpson, Coulthard, Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, Andersen, Moreton-Robinson, Trask, LaRocque); first-hand reading is partial and listed in the scope note (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md). Indigenous-authored historiography of 2018–24 is not yet surveyed beyond the History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) and Smith's 2022 conversation. Earlier basis: reviewed through 2000 in the original 1920–2000 experiment.

continuation.basis: One continuous field interval would conflate independently rooted practices. Lack of a bar does not imply those practices ceased.

chronology.interpretation: Show separate witnesses and interventions without joining them into one continuous academic-field bar. Keep manuscript creation, later editions, translations and collaborative practice distinct; the oldest witness is not the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge.
retain: Plural nations/traditions and community, university and collaborator positions; no common European-theory origin.
All 33 existing strands remain; this minimum pilot event set is not a replacement roster or complete chronology.
Reviewed through 2017 for part 2 (revision 1.201, 2026-10-27); 2018–24 not yet surveyed.
unresolved: If adding growth-phase intervals, name the specific region/institutions/methods and source them. Do not convert the broad 1970s–90s label into a universal shared phase.

audra_simpson.label: Audra Simpson
audra_simpson.date_label: “On Ethnographic Refusal” 2007 · Mohawk Interruptus 2014 · “The Ruse of Consent” 2017
audra_simpson.description: An anthropologist of Kahnawà:ke Mohawk nationhood whose method has become a resource for historians. In 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007) she proposed 'a sharp move away from the ethno-historical/salvage paradigm that evacuates theory' from Iroquois studies, which since Morgan had sought 'to authenticate cultural forms rather than analyse them', and she made refusal a method: ethnography as a calculus 'of what you need to know and what I refuse to write in'. History-writing, she argued, 'naturalises this occupation'; her own analysis reaches back through colonial membership law. Indigenous contexts are 'never properly "post-colonial"'. Mohawk Interruptus (2014), as Nicoll's review quotes it, carries the argument into Kahnawà:ke's migrations and into Morgan and Parker's ethnology, which became 'a regulatory body of knowledge' used 'to adjudicate claims to land'.
audra_simpson.representative_figures_and_works: Audra Simpson; 'Paths Toward a Mohawk Nation' (2001); 'To the Reserve and Back Again' (PhD, McGill, 2003); 'On the Logic of Discernment' (2007); 'On Ethnographic Refusal: Indigeneity, "Voice" and Colonial Citizenship' (2007); Mohawk Interruptus: Political Life Across the Borders of Settler States (2014); 'The Ruse of Consent and the Anatomy of "Refusal"' (2017).
audra_simpson.scope_note: Read in full: 'On Ethnographic Refusal' (2007). Mohawk Interruptus (2014) is known through Nicoll's review essay (2015), which quotes it with page numbers, and through the Duke page; 'The Ruse of Consent' (2017) at abstract level. In the texts read she does not criticise Wolfe; he appears only as a supporting citation (2007, n. 3). In Canadian History PhDs: 34 citing theses; share 0.3% in 2000–09 and 4.1% in 2018–25 (History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23).

glen_coulthard.label: Glen Sean Coulthard
glen_coulthard.date_label: Subjects of Empire? (PhD) 2009 · Red Skin, White Masks 2014
glen_coulthard.description: A political theorist whose critique of recognition is read by historians of colonial Canada. His 2009 dissertation, the basis of Red Skin, White Masks (2014), set out 'to challenge the now commonplace assumption that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition', using Fanon's critique of Hegel against the liberal recognition that Charles Taylor defended. Reworking Marx's primitive accumulation, he argued that 'the history and experience of dispossession, not proletarianization' had shaped relations with the Canadian state, and that Indigenous anti-colonialism is 'a struggle primarily inspired by and oriented around the question of land'. His alternative, self-recognition, means 'critically revaluating, reconstructing and redeploying Indigenous cultural forms'. He named Taiaiake Alfred, with James Tully, as a mentor.
glen_coulthard.representative_figures_and_works: Glen Sean Coulthard; Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the 'Politics of Recognition' in Canada (PhD, University of Victoria, 2009); Red Skin, White Masks: Rejecting the Colonial Politics of Recognition (2014; foreword by Taiaiake Alfred).
glen_coulthard.scope_note: Read in part: the 2009 dissertation (abstract; introduction pp. 1–2, 11–20, 27–28; chapter openings pp. 74–75, 158–160). The 2014 book is unread at first hand; its p. 125 is known through Englert (2020). emma_larocque.label: Emma LaRocque
emma_larocque.date_label: Defeathering the Indian 1975 · dissertation 1999 · When the Other Is Me 2011
emma_larocque.description: A scholar whose criticism of Canadian historical writing began with school textbooks. Her 1974 research for Alberta found 'endless layers of stereotypes … particularly in history and social studies' and led to Defeathering the Indian (1975). Her 1999 dissertation named its targets. James Walker's survey of Canadian historical writing was 'eye-opening and ground-breaking' but 'does not go deep enough', for 'Canadian historiography is not that benign'. Trigger's foreword to Sioui's Autohistory showed 'a language of containment'. The 'neo cross-cultural approach' of Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk framed 'all things Native' as 'cultural differences'. Scholars, 'especially historians and literary critics', must 'comprehend the noxious nature of colonization before dismissing utterances of decolonization'. She drew on Memmi, Fanon and Said, and on Howard Adams's 'White Ideal'. When the Other Is Me (2011) is the revised book.
emma_larocque.representative_figures_and_works: Emma LaRocque; Defeathering the Indian (1975); Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD, University of Manitoba, 1999); When the Other Is Me: Native Resistance Discourse, 1850–1990 (2011).
emma_larocque.scope_note: Read: 1999 dissertation, PDF pp. 8, 11, 21, 29, 34, 37–38, 47, 54, 70, 118–119, 135–136, 249. chris_andersen.label: Chris Andersen
chris_andersen.description: A sociologist whose 'Métis' (2014) challenges the understanding of Métis as 'mixed'. Scholars of 'Métis histories, literatures, and politics' are drawn to 'simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity'; to the question 'Have not fur trade historians … already extensively documented numerous instances of Métis mixedness?' he answers that 'the racialization of the Métis has never begun nor ended with us', but belonged to colonial projects to 'usurp all the Indigenous territories' on which Canada was built. Peoplehood rests instead on 'a "national core" historically located in Red River', and 'History is thus a crucial resource in Indigenous claims to peoplehood'. He draws on the historian Brenda Macdougall. His 2009 essay asked Indigenous studies to start from 'density' rather than 'difference', using the disciplines, history among them, that communities themselves use.
chris_andersen.representative_figures_and_works: Chris Andersen; with Brendan Hokowhitu, 'Whiteness: Naivety, Void and Control' (2007); 'Critical Indigenous Studies: From Difference to Density' (2009); 'Métis': Race, Recognition, and the Struggle for Indigenous Peoplehood (2014).
chris_andersen.scope_note: Read: the introduction of the 2014 book (pp. 3–20, publisher sample) and the 2009 article in part. The fur-trade historians he names are in chapter 1, unread; the critique edge to the fur-trade-families approach is drafted by the editors of Indigenous–newcomer relations. In the History PhD citation graph (release 2026-10-23) the book enters the Canadian Indigenous neighbourhood in 2015–19 and the settler-colonial neighbourhood in 2020–25.

haunani_kay_trask.label: Haunani-Kay Trask
haunani_kay_trask.date_label: Review of Linnekin 1986 · “Natives and Anthropologists” 1991 · From a Native Daughter 1993, revised 1999
haunani_kay_trask.description: A scholar of Hawaiian sovereignty whose 1991 reply to Roger Keesing is a founding exchange over who may interpret the Native past. Keesing had argued that Pacific nationalists idealise and 'invent' their pasts. Trask answered with 'solid evidence from Native forms of history-genealogy', charged that Keesing, 'with many Western academics', assumed that 'Natives don't know very much', and insisted 'We do not need, nor do we want to be "liberated" from our past'. She named Lilikalā Kameʻeleihiwa among the Native historians Keesing had not read. Keesing replied that her 'insider' versus 'outsider' dichotomy was 'a great leap backward'; Linnekin, that 'Traditions are neither genuine nor spurious'. Kauanui (2016) credits her essay on 'settlers of color' in Hawaiʻi as an earlier settler-colonial analysis.
haunani_kay_trask.representative_figures_and_works: Haunani-Kay Trask (1949–2021); review of Linnekin, Children of the Land (Hawaiian Journal of History, 1986); 'Natives and Anthropologists: The Colonial Struggle' (1991); From a Native Daughter: Colonialism and Sovereignty in Hawaiʻi (1993; revised 1999); 'Settlers of Color and "Immigrant" Hegemony' (Amerasia, 2000).
haunani_kay_trask.scope_note: Read in full: 'Natives and Anthropologists' (1991) and Keesing's reply; Linnekin's reply in part. From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999) is known through the publisher's description; the 1987 essay of that title and the 2000 essay are unread. winona_wheeler.label: Winona Wheeler
winona_wheeler.date_label: 'The Othering of Indigenous History' 1998 · 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' 2005 · 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' 2010 · Shekon Neechie 2018 · open letter 2021
winona_wheeler.description: Historian of Cree oral tradition and of the academy's treatment of Indigenous history. In 1998 she argued that historians of 'Indian–White relations', relying on the records of one side, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist frame. Her method writing treats Indigenous oral history 'as source and method in scholarly research': elders 'are not official documents; they are human beings and teachers', and the historian 'develops reciprocal relationships with them'. Oral historians, she argues, must learn how knowledge keepers establish their sources ('a traditional footnote'), and the historian's task is 'to apply the teachings that guide the learning, keeping, and transmission of Indigenous knowledge' (2010). She learned from Stan Cuthand, Ahenakew's protégé, and draws on Ahenakew's published account of Old Men as historians. Leddy (2010) opens her account of community-based history with Wheeler's words on knowledge 'by way of relationships'. She serves on the managing board of Shekon Neechie (2018).
winona_wheeler.representative_figures_and_works: Winona Wheeler (b. 1958; published as Winona Stevenson in the 1990s); 'Indigenous Voices, Indigenous Histories, Part I: The Othering of Indigenous History' (Saskatchewan History, 1998); 'Reflections on the Social Relations of Indigenous Oral History' (in Walking a Tightrope, 2005); 'Cree Intellectual Traditions in History' (in The West and Beyond, 2010). University of Saskatchewan (Native/Indigenous Studies) from 1988; First Nations University of Canada from 1996.

brenda_macdougall.label: Brenda Macdougall
brenda_macdougall.date_label: One of the Family 2010 · Clio Prize 2011 · 'Ways of Knowing' symposium 2018 · open letter 2021
brenda_macdougall.description: Historian of Métis family and community in the northwest. One of the Family (2010) set out 'to contribute … to the development of methodologies and models by which we could interpret historical documents in a manner that reflected the perspectives, realities, and experiences of Aboriginal communities'. She read fur-trade, mission and scrip records through wahkootowin, a concept she credits to Métis Elder Maria Campbell and frames as a Cree worldview of 'relatedness' that 'did not appear in any of the historical records'. Against a historiography 'overly preoccupied with race at the expense of culture', she showed Métis people 'actively involved in becoming, rather than passively awaiting identity transmission through external forces and trauma'. In 2018 she co-hosted a symposium on Métis-specific research methods.
brenda_macdougall.representative_figures_and_works: Brenda Macdougall; One of the Family: Metis Culture in Nineteenth-Century Northwestern Saskatchewan (UBC Press, 2010); 'Ways of Knowing: Promising New Directions for Métis Research' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). University of Saskatchewan (BA 1994, PhD 2005); University of Ottawa, Chair in Métis Studies from 2010.

robert_alexander_innes.label: Robert Alexander Innes
robert_alexander_innes.date_label: Oral history methods 1999–2000 · insider/outsider 2009 · Elder Brother and the Law of the People 2013 · 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' 2018 · open letter 2021
robert_alexander_innes.description: Historian of Cowessess First Nation, kinship and treaty land, and a critic of how historians have written the 1880s starvation policy. In 2018 he wrote that neither historians nor the Canadian government had acknowledged the starvation deaths of the early 1880s in Treaty 4 territory as genocide, and that historians who agreed the policy killed many had not tried to count the dead. Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research had done that work. Historical records, he argued, do not tell a story by themselves, and decolonizing history can simply mean asking the right questions and looking in the right places. Against Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), he held that Edgar Dewdney bore responsibility and that Daschuk misrepresented Tobias, Lux and Titley, whom he cites. Earlier he wrote on oral history methods in Native Studies and on insider research; he conceived Shekon Neechie (2018).
robert_alexander_innes.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Alexander Innes; 'Oral History Methods in Native Studies' (Oral History Forum, 1999–2000); 'Wait a Second. Who Are You Anyways?' (AIQ, 2009); Elder Brother and the Law of the People: Contemporary Kinship and Cowessess First Nation (UMP, 2013); 'Historians and Indigenous Genocide in Saskatchewan' and 'Clearing the Plains of Accountability' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). University of Saskatchewan (Indigenous Studies); McMaster University (2021).
robert_alexander_innes.scope_note: Read in full: the two Shekon Neechie essays of 21 June 2018 (the first also reposted on Active History, 12 June 2019; that page returned 403); USask News on Shekon Neechie (2018); the 2021 open letter. mary_jane_logan_mccallum.label: Mary Jane Logan McCallum
mary_jane_logan_mccallum.date_label: 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' 2009 · Indigenous Women, Work, and History 2014 · 'Words for Reading Indigenous Health History' 2017 · 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' 2018 · open letter 2021
mary_jane_logan_mccallum.description: Historian of Indigenous labour, health and archives. Indigenous Women, Work, and History (2014) follows domestic workers, hairdressers, community health representatives and nurses through state placement programmes, 1940–80; her reviewer Carol Williams notes that she worked with nursing associations who 'granted full access to records', and that her conclusion 'reflects on the professional status and glaring absence of Indigenous historians in academia'. Writing in 2018, she treats archives as sites of possibility and contestation for Indigenous historians: Indian Affairs records were made without Indigenous knowledge or consent, yet remain vital to Indigenous history. She describes interpreting such records together with others rather than alone, and hopes for Indigenous roles in making and keeping records. She sits on the managing board of Shekon Neechie.
mary_jane_logan_mccallum.representative_figures_and_works: Mary Jane Logan McCallum (b. 1974); 'Indigenous Labor and Indigenous History' (AIQ, 2009); Indigenous Women, Work, and History, 1940–1980 (UMP, 2014); 'Starvation, Experimentation, Segregation, and Trauma' (CHR, 2017); 'Indigenous People, Archives and History' (Shekon Neechie, 2018). Professor of History and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous People, History and Archives, University of Winnipeg.
